strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in audio-text retrieval evaluation: the mismatch between caption-style benchmark queries and realistic user search behavior (questions, commands, tags, paraphrases, exclusions).

Contributes a well-structured UIQ taxonomy (Conversational, Reformulation, Exclusionary) and releases three benchmark datasets (AudioCaps-UIQ, Clotho-UIQ, MECAT-UIQ) with both human and LLM-based quality validation.

Proposes novel and well-motivated discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, ∆-Rank) that go beyond standard R@k to explicitly measure suppression of acoustically similar but semantically distinct hard negatives, illustrated clearly via Figure 3.

Conducts a rigorous and unusually thorough data-leakage analysis between WavCaps and AudioCaps/Clotho (17.7% and 61.0% overlap respectively), and appropriately introduces MECAT as a leakage-free evaluation set — a valuable methodological contribution to the field.

Extensive experimentation across three backbones (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B/7B), multiple datasets, and many query types, with detailed appendices covering implementation, efficiency, prompts, and additional metrics, supporting reproducibility.
Reports results honestly, including cases where OEA underperforms M2D-CLAP (standard T2A, Question/Keyphrase/Paraphrase UIQ types), rather than overstating uniform superiority.
weaknesses: The headline T2T 'dominance' result is somewhat unsurprising and possibly not an apples-to-apples comparison: an LLM backbone with billions of parameters is compared against CLAP's lightweight text towers on a text-to-text task, which is a different setting from the paper's stated audio-text retrieval goal; the practical relevance of this caption-based pipeline (requiring an additional, unevaluated audio-captioning step) is not empirically validated end-to-end.

Absolute hard-negative discrimination performance remains low for all models (HNSR@10 around 30-35%), so while the reported relative improvement is notable, the practical significance of 'substantially superior' discrimination is questionable given both models still fail on the majority of exclusionary queries.

UIQ benchmark quality validation relies on a small sample (75 audio clips, 675 ratings) relative to the full 13,053-query benchmark, and queries are generated by a single LLM (GPT-5.1) under vocabulary-grounding constraints, raising concerns about diversity and representativeness that are only partially mitigated by length-distribution comparisons to real Freesound queries.

The hard negative mining pipeline is seeded by MGA-CLAP embeddings and filtered by BGE, which are the same models being compared against or closely related in spirit to baselines used in the discrimination evaluation, creating some circularity risk that human verification only partially addresses.

Results do not scale monotonically with backbone size (7B does not consistently outperform 3B, and even underperforms Nemo3B on some MECAT metrics), which weakens the narrative that larger/more capable LLM backbones straightforwardly translate to better retrieval-relevant semantic understanding.

No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported for the reported percentage-point and relative-improvement claims, making it hard to assess whether differences (e.g., +4.3%p HNSR@10) are robust versus noise across query/backbone variants.

OEA's efficiency profile is substantially worse than CLAP baselines (10-20x more GPU memory, several-fold higher latency), which is acknowledged but somewhat understates the practical deployment cost trade-off relative to the modest average performance gains.

The core modeling contribution (LoRA-tuned multimodal LLM backbone as a unified dual-purpose text/audio embedding model) is architecturally incremental relative to existing text-embedding-from-LLM approaches, with the paper's novelty concentrated more in the benchmark/metrics than the model itself.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and underexplored problem: standard audio-text retrieval benchmarks rely on caption-style queries that poorly reflect real-world search behavior (questions, commands, tags, paraphrases, negations).

The UIQ benchmark (five query types across three categories) is a reasonable and useful evaluation resource, validated with both human annotation and LLM-based scoring, and the authors commit to releasing it.

The hard-negative mining pipeline (acoustic similarity + semantic dissimilarity filtering + human verification) and the accompanying discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, Δ-Rank) are a thoughtful way to expose a blind spot of standard R@k metrics that only check retrieval, not suppression of confusable distractors.

The data-leakage analysis (Appendix B) is a valuable and honest contribution, quantifying substantial WavCaps/AudioCaps/Clotho overlap and motivating the use of MECAT as a leakage-free benchmark — this kind of rigor is uncommon and strengthens the credibility of the cross-domain claims.

Experiments span three backbones (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B/7B) and four CLAP baselines across three datasets, providing reasonably broad coverage, and efficiency/latency analysis is included for practical deployment considerations.
weaknesses: The central positive claim of "dominant T2T retrieval" is not really a fair architectural comparison: OEA uses the full billion-parameter LLM as a text encoder on both sides, while CLAP baselines use much smaller dedicated text encoders. This confound (parameter count / capacity mismatch, not a special multimodal contribution) is not controlled for or discussed adequately, making the +22% headline number potentially unsurprising rather than an interesting finding about LLM audio-text alignment specifically.

On the primary T2A retrieval task (the actual stated goal of the paper), OEA does not surpass M2D-CLAP on the most-used benchmark (AudioCaps, 72.6% vs 77.1% R@5) and only wins narrowly/inconsistently on Clotho and MECAT depending on variant — the framing as "comparable performance" downplays this asymmetric picture, and the paper leans heavily on secondary metrics (T2T, HNSR) to claim superiority.

The absolute improvement in hard-negative discrimination, while directionally consistent, is fairly modest (34.6% vs 30.3% HNSR@10) and is described with amplifying language ("substantially superior", "dominant") not clearly warranted by the effect size; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported anywhere in the paper for any comparison.

The scaling analysis (Appendix J) shows that the 7B backbone does not consistently outperform the 3B backbone, and in some cases underperforms Nemotron-3B — this undercuts the paper's core mechanistic story that "LLM backbones provide superior semantic understanding," since if that mechanism were driving the gains, scale should help more consistently.

UIQ generation depends entirely on a single LLM (GPT-5.1) under vocabulary-grounding constraints, and while human/LLM validation scores are reported, the sample size for human validation is very small (75 samples, 9 annotators, 675 ratings) relative to the full released benchmark (13k+ queries), leaving open questions about whether the full generated set is representative of real user query diversity beyond token-length matching.

On standard UIQ retrieval (Table 4), M2D-CLAP actually achieves the best overall average (47.76 vs. OEA's best 47.18), and OEA's advantages are confined to a narrow subset (Imperative queries, hard-negative discrimination) — the abstract and conclusion arguably overstate the breadth of OEA's superiority relative to what the full results support.

The evaluation and generation pipeline both leverage LLMs (GPT-5.1 for generation, Claude Opus 4.5 for validation) that may share stylistic priors with the OEA backbones (also LLM-based), raising a subtle concern about whether some of OEA's relative advantage on LLM-generated UIQs reflects genuine query-understanding robustness versus stylistic alignment between generator and encoder families; this is only partially addressed via the Freesound length-distribution comparison.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: standard audio-text retrieval benchmarks (AudioCaps, Clotho) rely on caption-style queries that do not reflect real-world search behavior, and the paper backs this claim with citations and its own analysis.

The data leakage analysis (Appendix B) is a genuinely valuable and under-appreciated contribution: quantifying 17.7% overlap between AudioCaps test and WavCaps, and 61% overlap between Clotho and WavCaps, exposes a real contamination problem in prior CLAP training pipelines and motivates the use of MECAT as a leakage-free benchmark.

The UIQ benchmark (five query types across three linguistically-motivated categories) is systematically constructed and validated through both human annotation (9 annotators, 675 ratings) and LLM-based evaluation, with reported agreement statistics, which strengthens confidence in benchmark quality.

The proposed discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, Delta-Rank) meaningfully complement standard R@k by capturing whether models actually suppress acoustically confusable distractors, addressing a real gap in existing negation/exclusion retrieval literature (NevIR, ExcluIR).

Experiments span multiple backbones (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B/7B) and three datasets, with reasonably thorough ablations in the appendix (efficiency, scaling behavior, per-dataset UIQ breakdowns), supporting the generality claims to a degree.

The paper is transparent about limitations (single LLM generator for UIQs, dependency on multimodal backbones, memory footprint) and provides a nuanced, honest 'practical decision rule' for when to prefer OEA vs. M2D-CLAP rather than overclaiming universal superiority.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'comparable T2A performance' is a somewhat generous characterization: Table 2 shows M2D-CLAP substantially outperforms all OEA variants on AudioCaps (e.g., 77.13% vs. 72.64% R@5, an ~4.5pp gap), and OEA's advantage on Clotho/MECAT is real but not uniformly dominant either. This nuance is somewhat flattened in the abstract/intro framing.

The T2T 'dominance' result is architecturally almost guaranteed rather than a deep finding: OEA uses the same large LLM backbone to encode both queries and captions, whereas CLAP baselines use lightweight, much smaller dedicated text encoders. This is a meaningful practical comparison for caption-based pipelines, but calling it evidence of 'superior semantic understanding' somewhat overstates what is largely an artifact of parameter-count and architecture asymmetry.

The absolute performance on hard-negative discrimination remains low for all models (e.g., TFR@10 around 7.5%–10.1%), meaning the reported '+34.7% relative' and '+4.3pp' improvements represent modest absolute gains on a task where all systems still perform quite poorly; the framing sometimes emphasizes relative percentages that can appear more impressive than the absolute numbers warrant.

There is a potential circularity/bias concern in the hard-negative mining pipeline: hard negatives are mined using MGA-CLAP embeddings for acoustic similarity, and MGA-CLAP is also one of the baselines being evaluated on this benchmark, which could differentially advantage or disadvantage certain models depending on embedding-space idiosyncrasies not fully explored.

UIQ generation constrains query length to within ±2 words of original captions and requires vocabulary grounding to reused caption wording; this is a reasonable control but pushes most UIQ types (especially paraphrase, question) toward much longer and more caption-like text than real user queries, which per the cited Freesound analysis average only 1.8 tokens—raising questions about how well the benchmark's 'user-intent' framing actually captures real-world query brevity despite the authors' Appendix I discussion.

Human validation of the UIQ benchmark is relatively small-scale (9 annotators, 15 audio clips per dataset, 75 total samples), limiting the statistical robustness of the benchmark-quality claims despite decent reported agreement.

The proposed explanation for OEA's negation/exclusion advantage (LLM exposure to negation during instruction pretraining preserving compositional structure via attention) is plausible but not directly tested via targeted ablation or probing; it remains speculative rather than empirically isolated from confounds like backbone scale or general language competence.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals, paired tests) is reported for the numerous pairwise comparisons across many models/datasets/metrics, making it harder to assess whether some of the smaller reported gaps (e.g., HNSR@10 differences of a few points) are robust rather than noise.

The MECAT dataset citation appears anonymized/incomplete in the reference list ('Anonymous Wu and 1 others. 2025'), which is unusual for a work being used as a core evaluation benchmark and raises minor concerns about full traceability/reproducibility of that resource.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in audio-text retrieval evaluation: standard benchmarks use caption-style queries that do not reflect real-world search behavior, and the paper systematically motivates this with prior literature (Weck & Font, Selvakumar et al.).

Introduces and releases three new UIQ benchmark datasets (AudioCaps-UIQ, Clotho-UIQ, MECAT-UIQ) spanning five query formulations, along with code, checkpoints, and a web demo, providing a useful community resource.

Rigorous data-leakage analysis (Appendix B) quantifying WavCaps overlap with AudioCaps (17.7%) and Clotho (61.0%) test sets is a valuable and often-overlooked methodological contribution, and the use of MECAT as a leakage-free benchmark strengthens the evaluation's validity.
Proposes well-motivated discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, ∆-Rank) that expose a real blind spot of standard R@k metrics for exclusionary queries, illustrated clearly (Figure 3).

Extensive and unusually self-critical mechanism ablations (Appendix O) that decompose the source of OEA's hard-negative discrimination gains via controlled experiments (audio-only separation, negation on/off, word-shuffle controls, cross-model shuffle controls) with proper paired statistical testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank), leading the authors to revise/qualify their own hypothesis rather than overclaim.
Reasonably broad experimental coverage: three backbones, four CLAP baselines, three evaluation datasets, and detailed per-query-type breakdowns in the appendix.
UIQ benchmark quality is validated with both human annotation and LLM-based scoring, with reported inter-rater/agreement statistics.
weaknesses: The architecture itself (shared LLM backbone + LoRA adapters + modality-specific projection heads trained with symmetric InfoNCE) is a relatively straightforward application of existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning and contrastive learning techniques, offering limited technical/methodological novelty.

The headline T2T improvement (+22%) is a somewhat unfair/expected comparison: CLAP's lightweight text encoders were never designed for text-to-text semantic matching, so an LLM backbone naturally excels here; this result says more about using an LLM as a sentence encoder than about audio-text retrieval per se.

Core T2A retrieval results show only "comparable" performance to M2D-CLAP (and worse on AudioCaps specifically), while OEA's inference cost is substantially higher (audio encoding latency 164–667 ms/clip vs. 30–108 ms/clip for CLAP baselines, per Appendix K), raising questions about the practical value of the proposed approach despite the reported gains.

The magnitude of the hard-negative discrimination improvement (+4.3pp HNSR@10) is modest, and the mechanism ablations ultimately show that OEA's text-side order sensitivity is not a unique or novel mechanism but a general property shared with (and in one case weaker than) CLAP baselines — undercutting the strength of the discrimination claim as a distinguishing contribution.

UIQ benchmark quality validation is based on a very small sample (75 of 13,053 queries, ~0.6%), and both the generation (GPT-5.1) and validation (Claude Opus 4.5) rely on proprietary, potentially non-reproducible/non-static LLMs, raising reproducibility concerns and some circularity in using an LLM to validate LLM-generated content.

No empirical comparison of UIQ query statistics (e.g., token length distributions) against real-world query logs (e.g., Freesound queries), despite motivating the work with exactly this kind of mismatch; the connection to genuine real-world search behavior remains largely assumed rather than demonstrated.

The hard-negative mining pipeline depends on MGA-CLAP for candidate retrieval, which is also one of the evaluated baselines, creating a potential circularity/confound that the paper acknowledges but only partially mitigates through threshold calibration rather than independent validation.

Statistical significance for the main comparative results (Tables 2–4) is not reported, in contrast to the appendix ablations which do include significance testing; this makes it harder to assess whether some of the smaller headline gaps (e.g., UIQ category differences) are robust.

strengths: The paper performs an unusually thorough and intellectually honest mechanism analysis (Appendix O): rather than resting on the initial hypothesis that OEA's LLM backbone understands negation/exclusion semantics, the authors run cross-model shuffle controls and explicitly show that order-sensitivity is a general property shared with CLAP text encoders, and that the real driver is audio-embedding separability. This kind of self-correcting ablation is commendable and rare.

The data leakage analysis (Appendix B) quantifying WavCaps overlap with AudioCaps (17.7%) and Clotho (61.0%) test sets is a genuinely useful contribution to the field, and the inclusion of MECAT as a leakage-free benchmark is a valuable methodological corrective that could benefit future audio retrieval research.

Broad experimental coverage: three backbone architectures, three evaluation datasets, multiple CLAP baselines, and an extensive appendix including UIQ human+LLM validation, hard-negative mining calibration, inference efficiency, and scaling analyses.

The proposed UIQ taxonomy and discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, Delta-Rank) address a real and under-explored gap (caption-style vs. real-world queries) and are reasonably well defined with an illustrative distinction from standard R@k.
Benchmarks, code, and checkpoints are released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline claims in the abstract/intro are considerably stronger than what the body and appendices actually support: the "dominant" T2T result is an apples-to-oranges comparison (large LLM backbone vs. lightweight CLAP text encoder on a text-only matching task that is not the paper's core retrieval objective), and the "substantially superior" hard-negative discrimination claim is walked back in Appendix O to a much more qualified story (shared order-sensitivity weaknesses, exclusion clause actually hurts suppression for every model including OEA, and the gain is confined to specific metrics/checkpoints).

On the primary task (text-to-audio retrieval) and on 3 of 5 UIQ query types (Question, Keyphrase, Paraphrase), OEA does not outperform M2D-CLAP; M2D-CLAP wins overall mean UIQ R@5. The paper's framing selectively emphasizes the subset of metrics where OEA wins (Imperative, HNSR) as the main finding, which risks overstating the contribution.

The core architecture (LoRA-adapted multimodal LLM as unified text/audio encoder) is a relatively incremental engineering extension of existing omni-LLM and retrieval-tuning techniques rather than a novel method, and is similar in spirit to concurrent work (Omni-Embed-Nemotron) already used as one of its own backbones.

UIQ benchmark quality assurance is only sample-based (75 of 13,053 queries, ~0.6%), generated from a single LLM (GPT-5.1) without exhaustive human review; while this is disclosed, it limits confidence in benchmark validity at scale, especially given the paper's own emphasis on the importance of rigorous evaluation design.

The length-matching constraint (±2 words of original captions) used to generate UIQs is in tension with the paper's own motivating evidence that real-world queries average only 1.8 tokens (Weck and Font), raising doubts about how well the UIQ benchmark actually captures the real-world query distribution it is designed to emulate.

No variance/significance reporting (multiple seeds, confidence intervals) for the main results tables (T2A, T2T, UIQ); statistical tests appear only in the post-hoc mechanism ablations, making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., +4.3 pts HNSR@10) are robust rather than noise, especially given fairly small absolute margins.

Training data and potential leakage asymmetries between OEA and CLAP baselines are not fully controlled for—OEA is trained on WavCaps/AudioCaps/Clotho with blocklisting applied only to OEA's own training, but it is unclear whether the CLAP baselines' original training pipelines had comparable decontamination, complicating fair comparison.

strengths: Rigorous data leakage analysis (Appendix B) is a genuine and valuable contribution — the paper quantifies substantial contamination between WavCaps and standard AudioCaps/Clotho test sets (17.7% and 61.0% overlap respectively) and introduces MECAT as a leakage-free evaluation, which strengthens the credibility of the reported generalization claims.

The UIQ benchmark addresses a real and previously under-examined gap between caption-style retrieval benchmarks and natural user search behavior, with five linguistically motivated query types and both human and LLM-based validation (Table 1/6), improving reproducibility and usefulness for the community.

The proposed HNSR/TFR/Δ-Rank metrics meaningfully expose a blind spot of standard R@k metrics — the inability to measure suppression of acoustically confusable distractors — and the hard-negative mining pipeline is calibrated via human listening rather than relying solely on model similarity.

The mechanism ablations in Appendix O are unusually careful and scientifically honest: the authors test and ultimately reject their own initial hypothesis (negation understanding from instruction pretraining) in favor of a more nuanced, evidence-based account (audio-embedding separability plus generic order-sensitivity shared with CLAP), with appropriate paired statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p-values reported).
Broad experimental coverage across three backbones, three datasets, and multiple baselines, with released benchmarks, code, and checkpoints supporting reproducibility.

Nuanced, non-cherry-picked reporting: the paper openly states that M2D-CLAP wins on T2A and overall UIQ average, rather than claiming blanket superiority, which increases trustworthiness of the findings.
weaknesses: The core architectural contribution (LoRA-adapted shared multimodal LLM backbone + projection heads + symmetric InfoNCE) is fairly incremental relative to existing text-embedding-from-LLM and unified-encoder retrieval literature; the paper's novelty rests primarily on the benchmark/metric contributions rather than the model itself.

The headline T2T improvement (+22%) is somewhat expected/unsurprising, since it largely reflects comparing a billion-parameter LLM text encoder against CLAP's much smaller, contrastively-optimized text towers — the comparison is not fully controlled for capacity, making the magnitude of superiority less informative than presented.

Absolute improvement in the primary discrimination metric is modest (HNSR@10: 34.6% vs 30.3%, a 4.3-point gap), and this comparison lacks reported statistical significance/confidence intervals in the main results tables (Table 4/15), unlike the more careful ablations in Appendix O.

OEA does not dominate on the primary/traditional T2A retrieval task (M2D-CLAP leads clearly on AudioCaps, Table 2) nor on average UIQ performance (Table 4, M2D-CLAP 47.76% vs OEA's best 47.18%), somewhat undercutting the strength of the 'robust retrieval' framing in the abstract/title.

UIQ benchmark quality is validated on only 75 of 13,053 released queries (a small sample), and generation relies on a single LLM (GPT-5.1) with vocabulary-grounding constraints that may not fully reflect real-world query distributions (acknowledged by authors but still a soundness limitation).

Inference cost is substantially higher for OEA (e.g., 160–670 ms/clip vs 30–110 ms/clip for CLAP baselines, per Table 16), a significant practical limitation that is relegated to an appendix rather than foregrounded in the main narrative.

The negation/exclusion-understanding mechanism, initially framed as a distinguishing strength, is ultimately shown (Ablation 3-X) to be a generic property shared with CLAP text encoders rather than unique to OEA, which somewhat weakens one of the paper's headline claims about 'superior semantic understanding' even though the authors appropriately caveat this in the final analysis.
